name: South Dravidian
defining_innovation: Krishnamurti's grouping of South-Central Dravidian (Telugu, Gondi) with South Dravidian I (Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam, Tulu), on shared changes in the vowels and in verb and pronoun morphology.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
South Dravidian takes in all four of the great literary Dravidian languages (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam) and more than 90 per cent of Dravidian speakers. Krishnamurti argued that South-Central Dravidian, the branch of Telugu and Gondi, shares an ancestor with South Dravidian I, the branch of Tamil and Kannada. Others see South-Central as closer to the Central languages, or as a bridge between them. That alternative appears on the tree as a dotted arc between Central and South-Central.

By the last centuries BCE, South Dravidian speakers were living in the kingdoms of the far south, and their languages begin to appear in inscriptions and poetry.

turning_points.title: South-Central and South Dravidian I part
turning_points.description: South Dravidian divides into South-Central Dravidian (Telugu, Gondi, Kui) and South Dravidian I (Tamil, Kannada, Malayalam, Tulu). Krishnamurti's date is approximate, and the grouping itself is disputed.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: South-Central with Central: Telugu, Gondi and Kui belong with the Central Dravidian languages, not with Tamil and Kannada
contested_classifications.evidence_for: South-Central and Central languages are neighbours across central India and share a number of features. Some earlier classifications, and some lexicostatistical studies, put them together.
contested_classifications.evidence_against: Krishnamurti identified innovations, such as changes in the vowel system and in the forms of pronouns and verbs, that South-Central shares only with South Dravidian I. Features shared with Central Dravidian can be explained as contact between neighbours. Most recent classifications follow Krishnamurti.

sources.citation: Krishnamurti, Bhadriraju. 2003. The Dravidian Languages. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Kolipakam, Vishnupriya, et al. 2018. A Bayesian phylogenetic study of the Dravidian language family. Royal Society Open Science 5.
